pos: adj. (pertaining to a prophet or to prophecy; of Christ's office as the Revealer of God)
etymology: Greek prophetes, one who speaks forth — from pro, before or forth, and phemi, to speak. The prophet's first work is not prediction but utterance on God's behalf.
biblical_def: The prophetical office is the first of Christ's three, and it is promised at Sinai: “The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken” (Deu 18:15), which Peter applies to Christ (Act 3:22). He claims it at Nazareth: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor” (Luk 4:18). He fulfils it as the final word: “God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son” (Heb 1:1–2). And He shares what He has received: “all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you” (John 15:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prophetical as containing prophecy, or foretelling future events; and prophet as one that foretells future events, and also a person illuminated, instructed or inspired by God to announce future events.
webster_full: PROPHETIC, PROPHETICAL, a. Containing prophecy; foretelling events; as prophetic writings.
2. Having the character of a prophet; as a prophetic voice.
PROPHET, n. One that foretells future events; a predicter; a foreteller.
2. In Scripture, a person illuminated, instructed or inspired by God to announce future events; as Moses, Elijah, David, Isaiah.
3. One who pretends to foretell; an imposter; as a false prophet.
scriptures: The LORD thy God will raise up unto thee a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken;
Act 3:22
For Moses truly said unto the fathers, A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me; him shall ye hear in all things whatsoever he shall say unto you.
Luk 4:18

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised,
Heb 1:1
God, who at sundry times and in divers manners spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets,
John 15:15
Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends; for all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you.
corruption_summary: The prophetic office is reduced to prediction, and its main business is speaking God's word into the present.
corruption_paragraphs: Prediction is a genuine part of the office and the Old Testament tests a prophet by it — if the thing follow not, the LORD hath not spoken it. But prediction is a minority of what the prophets actually did. Read Amos, Micah or Jeremiah and the bulk is indictment, call and covenant lawsuit: this is what you have done, this is what the LORD says about it, and this is what He requires. A church that thinks of prophecy chiefly as a calendar of future events will read the prophets badly and, worse, will listen for the wrong thing when the word is preached to it.

Hebrews 1:1–2 makes Christ's prophetic office final in a way that closes something. God spoke in divers manners by the prophets and has now spoken by a Son — not one more messenger in the line but the Heir, the brightness of His glory, through whom the worlds were made. The consequence is that a claim to fresh revelation of the same order is a claim that the last word was not last. This is why the Reformed have located Christ's continuing prophetic ministry in the Spirit's application of the written word, and why the pulpit is a serious place: the office is exercised now through the preaching of what has already been given.

The threefold office is one office and the parts interpret each other. A Christ who is Prophet only becomes a teacher of ethics and the cross becomes an example. A Christ who is Priest only becomes a transaction with no word attached. A Christ who is King only becomes power without mercy. He reveals God to us, He offers Himself for us, and He rules us — and the same Person does all three, which is why no one of them can be dropped without deforming the other two.
roots_summary: Greek prophetes (G4396), prophet; propheteia (G4394), prophecy; Hebrew nabi (H5030), prophet, spokesman; chazon (H2377), vision.
roots_lines: Hebrew nabi (H5030) — prophet, spokesman; Deuteronomy 18:15–22, Exodus 7:1, Amos 3:7.
Greek prophetes (G4396) — prophet; Acts 3:22–23, Matthew 21:11, Luke 24:19, Ephesians 4:11.
Greek propheteia (G4394) — prophecy; 2 Peter 1:20–21, 1 Corinthians 14:22, Revelation 19:10.
usage: “A Prophet… like unto me; unto him ye shall hearken” — promised at Sinai.
“Hath in these last days spoken unto us by his Son” — the last word, and it is a Person.
“All things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you”.

pos: adj. (double; of two parts — in Calvin, the twofold knowledge of God and of ourselves with which the Institutes open)
etymology: Old English twa, two, and -fald, fold. The AV uses it once, of the proselyte made “twofold more the child of hell” (Mat 23:15).
biblical_def: Calvin opens the Institutes by observing that nearly all true wisdom consists of two parts, the knowledge of God and the knowledge of ourselves, and that neither can be had without the other. Scripture keeps them joined: Job says “I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes” (Job 42:5–6); Isaiah sees the Lord high and lifted up and cries “Woe is me! for I am undone” (Isa 6:5); Peter, after the great catch, says “Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord” (Luk 5:8). The order runs from God outward: “in thy light shall we see light” (Psa 36:9). The AV's own use of the word is a warning (Mat 23:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines twofold as two of the same kind, or two different things existing together; double; as twofold nature, twofold sense.
webster_full: TWOFOLD, a. Two of the same kind, or two different things existing together; as twofold nature; twofold sense; twofold argument.
TWOFOLD, adv. In a double degree; as, to render twofold.
scriptures: Job 42:5
I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee.
Isa 6:5
Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts.
Luk 5:8
When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord.
Psa 36:9
For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light.
Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye compass sea and land to make one proselyte, and when he is made, ye make him twofold more the child of hell than yourselves.
corruption_summary: Self-knowledge is pursued apart from the knowledge of God, and what a man learns that way is either flattery or despair.
corruption_paragraphs: Calvin's argument is that the two knowledges are not merely both necessary but mutually conditioning, and the order matters. A man measuring himself against other men will always find someone worse and will grade himself accordingly; measured against the holiness of God he is undone. Isaiah 6 shows the mechanism in three verses: the prophet, a godly man by every human standard, sees the Lord and immediately says Woe is me. He had not learnt anything new about himself; he had acquired the standard by which the old facts became visible.

Run the other way, the corruption is subtler and more modern: an inward examination that never lifts its eyes. Endless self-analysis produces either self-loathing or self-justification, and both are forms of the same mistake, since both keep the self as the measure. Job 42 is instructive because Job's self-abhorrence arrives not through introspection — he had defended himself capably for thirty chapters — but through a vision of God who never once answers the question Job asked. The cure for a man's excessive interest in himself is rarely more thinking about himself.

The pastoral use is direct. When a believer is crushed by his own failure, the remedy is not a lower estimate of the sin but a larger sight of Christ; when he is complacent, the remedy is the same. Psalm 36:9 gives the principle: in thy light shall we see light — we do not see clearly and then look at God; we look at God and then see. Every honest self-knowledge the Bible records begins with a sight of Him.
roots_summary: Greek diplous (G1362), double, twofold; epiginosko (G1921), to know fully; Hebrew yada (H3045), to know; ma'as (H3988), to reject, abhor.
roots_lines: Greek diplous (G1362) — double, twofold; Matthew 23:15, 1 Timothy 5:17, Revelation 18:6.
Hebrew yada (H3045) — to know; Jeremiah 9:23–24, Hosea 6:3, Psalm 46:10.
Greek epiginosko (G1921) — to know fully, recognise; 1 Corinthians 13:12, Colossians 1:6.
usage: “Now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself” — the order, in one sentence.
“Woe is me! for I am undone” — said by a godly man who had just seen God.
“In thy light shall we see light” — we look at Him, and then we see.

pos: adj. (neither commanded nor forbidden; of things morally neutral in themselves — the adiaphora)
etymology: Latin indifferens, making no difference. “Things indifferent” was the technical phrase of the Reformation debates over ceremonies, vestments and days.
biblical_def: A thing indifferent is neither commanded nor forbidden, so that a believer may do it or leave it. Romans 14 is the charter: “One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” (Rom 14:5). The neutrality is real — “there is nothing unclean of itself” (Rom 14:14); “meat commendeth us not to God: for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse” (1Co 8:8). But it is bounded twice: by edification, “all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not” (1Co 10:23), and by conscience, since “whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Rom 14:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines indifferent as having no difference or distinction; neither good nor bad; having no influence or preponderating weight; of no account or importance.
webster_full: INDIFFERENT, a. Neutral; not inclined to one side, party or thing more than to another.
2. Unconcerned; feeling no interest, anxiety or care respecting anything.
3. Having no influence or preponderating weight; having no difference that gives a preference.
4. Neither good nor bad; of a middle state or quality; as an indifferent action.
5. Impartial; disinterested; as an indifferent judge.
scriptures: Rom 14:5
One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.
I know, and am persuaded by the Lord Jesus, that there is nothing unclean of itself: but to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean.
But meat commendeth us not to God: for neither, if we eat, are we the better; neither, if we eat not, are we the worse.
All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not.
And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin.
corruption_summary: The category collapses in both directions — everything is made a matter of conscience, or nothing is.
corruption_paragraphs: The first collapse is legalism, which promotes indifferent things into commands and then makes them terms of fellowship. Romans 14 was written to a church doing exactly that over meat and days, and Paul's ruling is startlingly permissive on the matter itself and severe about the treatment of the brother: let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not, and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth. The sin under correction is not the eating or the abstaining — both are allowed in the same paragraph — but the contempt in one direction and the censure in the other.

The second collapse is licence, which files everything under liberty and never asks the next question. Paul is careful to say twice that the lawful is not the whole calculation: all things are lawful, but all things edify not; all things are lawful, but I will not be brought under the power of any. A Christian who has established that a thing is permitted has finished the easy half of the deliberation. Whether it builds up, whether it enslaves, whether it wounds a weaker brother — those are the questions that remain, and none of them is answered by the permission.

Romans 14:23 gives the hinge that keeps the doctrine from being a licence for the doubtful: whatsoever is not of faith is sin. A man who acts against his own conscience sins even when the act itself is indifferent, because he has taught himself to act against conviction and will do it again in a matter that is not indifferent. This is why the strong may not simply argue the weak out of a scruple by force. Conscience is instructed by Scripture, patiently, and until it is instructed it must be obeyed.
roots_summary: Greek koinos (G2839), common, unclean; diakrino (G1252), to doubt, make a distinction; oikodomeo (G3618), to edify; exousia (G1849), liberty, right.
roots_lines: Greek koinos (G2839) — common, unclean; Romans 14:14, Acts 10:14–15, 11:8–9.
Greek diakrinomai (G1252) — to doubt, waver; Romans 14:23, James 1:6, Mark 11:23.
Greek exousia (G1849) — liberty, right; 1 Corinthians 8:9, 9:4–18, 10:23 context.
usage: “Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind” — his own, not his brother's.
“All things are lawful… but all things edify not” — the second half of the question.
“Whatsoever is not of faith is sin” — even when the act is indifferent.

pos: n. (fitness; propriety of behaviour or of worship; what becomes the occasion and the God being worshipped)
etymology: Latin decere, to be fitting, to become — the same root as decorum. Decency is not primness; it is fitness to the thing being done.
biblical_def: Decency is fitness, and Paul makes it the rule of public worship in a single verse: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). The ground is the character of God: “for God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints” (1Co 14:33). It bears on the appearance of things — “Judge in yourselves: is it comely that a woman pray unto God uncovered?” (1Co 11:13) — and on the body of Christ, where “our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness” (1Co 12:23). Outside the assembly it is a rule of walk: “let us walk honestly, as in the day” (Rom 13:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines decency as propriety of form in social intercourse, in words or behavior; opposed to rudeness, lewdness or indelicacy; and that which is becoming in words or actions.
webster_full: DECENCY, n. Propriety of form in social intercourse, in words or behavior, or in the external appearance of things; that which is becoming or fit.
2. Suitableness to character; propriety; opposed to rudeness or indecorum.
3. Modesty; propriety of behavior in relation to sex or delicacy.
DECENT, a. Becoming; fit; suitable, in words, behavior, dress and ceremony.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace, as in all churches of the saints.
Judge in yourselves: is it comely that a woman pray unto God uncovered?
And those members of the body, which we think to be less honourable, upon these we bestow more abundant honour; and our uncomely parts have more abundant comeliness.
Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying.
corruption_summary: Decency is used to canonise a congregation's habits, and it is used to dismiss the question entirely; both misread the verse.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 14:40 is the most abused verse in worship debates because it is quoted as though it settled particulars. It does not. It gives a principle — decently and in order — and the same chapter shows what Paul meant by it: not silence and not solemnity for its own sake, but that people speak one at a time, that what is said be understood, and that everything serve edification. A church appealing to this verse to defend the order of service it inherited has usually stopped reading at verse 40 and skipped the forty verses of argument that produce it.

The opposite abuse dispenses with the category, treating any concern for fitness as cold formalism and any spontaneity as life. But the ground Paul gives is theological, not aesthetic: God is not the author of confusion. What happens in an assembly says something about the God being worshipped, and a service that communicates chaos has made a statement, whatever the intention. The question is never whether a congregation has a form — it always has one — but whether the form it has fits the God it names.

Verse 33 supplies the corrective to a merely local decency: as in all churches of the saints. Paul appeals past Corinth's preferences to the practice of the wider church, which cuts against the congregation that regards its own customs as the standard, and equally against the innovator who owes nothing to anyone. Decency is not what this congregation is used to; it is what befits the God whom all the churches worship.
roots_summary: Greek euschemonos (G2156), decently, becomingly; taxis (G5010), order; akatastasia (G181), confusion, disorder; prepo (G4241), to be fitting, comely.
roots_lines: Greek euschemonos (G2156) — decently, honestly; 1 Corinthians 14:40, Romans 13:13, 1 Thessalonians 4:12.
Greek taxis (G5010) — order, arrangement; 1 Corinthians 14:40, Colossians 2:5, Hebrews 5:6.
Greek prepo (G4241) — to be becoming, seemly; 1 Corinthians 11:13, Ephesians 5:3, Titus 2:1, Hebrews 7:26.
usage: “Let all things be done decently and in order” — a principle, after forty verses of argument.
“God is not the author of confusion” — the ground is theological, not aesthetic.
“As in all churches of the saints” — past this congregation's preferences.

pos: adj. (contrary to; inconsistent with — in the confessions, of anything that contradicts the written Word)
etymology: Latin repugnare, to fight back, from re-, against, and pugnare, to fight. The confessional formula is that nothing is to be added “whether by new revelations of the Spirit, or traditions of men”, and nothing contrary or repugnant to Scripture may be received.
biblical_def: In confessional usage a thing is repugnant when it fights against the written Word. The test is stated by Isaiah: “To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them” (Isa 8:20). It is absolute even against the highest credentials: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8). It is guarded at both ends of the canon: “Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it” (Deu 4:2); “If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues” (Rev 22:18). And the Bereans applied it to an apostle (Act 17:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines repugnant as opposite; contrary; inconsistent; properly, disobedient; not consistent with; as, a proposition repugnant to the constitution.
webster_full: REPUGNANT, a. Opposite; contrary; properly, striving against.
2. Disobedient; not obsequious.
3. Contrary; inconsistent; as, a proposition may be repugnant to the constitution of the state.
REPUGNANCE, n. Opposition of mind; reluctance; unwillingness; contrariety or inconsistency.
scriptures: Isa 8:20
To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them.
Gal 1:8
But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.
Deu 4:2
Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the LORD your God which I command you.
For I testify unto every man that heareth the words of the prophecy of this book, If any man shall add unto these things, God shall add unto him the plagues that are written in this book:
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
corruption_summary: The test is applied to everyone else's doctrine and never to one's own, and the word slides from ‘contrary to Scripture’ to ‘distasteful to me’.
corruption_paragraphs: The confessional word means one specific thing: contradicting the written Word. Its modern sense — disgusting, offensive to feeling — is a different judgment altogether, and a great deal of confusion follows from running the two together. Doctrines that are repugnant in the modern sense are scattered through Scripture: election, eternal punishment, the wrath of God, the exclusivity of Christ. That a teaching offends is no evidence at all about whether it fights against the Word; the only way to find out is to go to the law and to the testimony, which is a labour rather than a reaction.

The discipline cuts both ways and its harder edge is inward. Galatians 1:8 includes the apostle himself in the anathema — though we, or an angel from heaven — which means Paul submitted his own future preaching to a standard outside himself. Acts 17:11 shows the Bereans doing the same thing from below, searching the scriptures daily to see whether the things an apostle told them were so, and being commended for it. A tradition, a confession, a favourite teacher or one's own settled convictions are all subject to the test, and the man who never finds anything of his own repugnant to Scripture has almost certainly stopped applying it.
roots_summary: Hebrew torah (H8451) and teudah (H8584), the law and the testimony; yasaph (H3254), to add; gara (H1639), to diminish; Greek anathema (G331), accursed.
roots_lines: Hebrew torah…teudah (H8451, H8584) — the law and the testimony; Isaiah 8:16, 8:20.
Greek anathema esto (G331) — let him be accursed; Galatians 1:8–9, 1 Corinthians 16:22.
Greek anakrino (G350) — to examine; Acts 17:11, 1 Corinthians 2:14–15.
usage: “If they speak not according to this word” — the test, and it is a labour.
“Though we, or an angel from heaven” — Paul under his own standard.
“Ye shall not add… neither shall ye diminish” — both directions guarded.

pos: adj. (folded in; unquestioning — in controversy, of a faith that assents to whatever the church holds without knowing what that is)
etymology: Latin implicitus, folded in, entangled. Rome's fides implicita allowed a layman to believe rightly by intending to believe whatever the church believed; the 1689 names it as a thing faith is not.
biblical_def: Implicit faith is assent without content — believing that whatever the church teaches is true, without knowing what it teaches. Scripture makes faith depend on a known object: “faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Rom 10:17). Christ rejects worship without knowledge outright: “Ye worship ye know not what: we know what we worship” (John 4:22), and Paul finds the same defect on an Athenian altar, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD (Act 17:23). The prophet names the cost: “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge” (Hos 4:6). And every believer is to be “ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you” (1Pe 3:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines implicit as, in a theological sense, resting on another's authority; trusting without doubting or reserve; as implicit faith, implicit confidence, implicit obedience.
webster_full: IMPLICIT, a. Infolded; entangled; complicated.
2. Implied; tacitly comprised; fairly to be understood, though not expressed.
3. Resting on another; trusting in the word or authority of another, without doubting or reserve, or without examining evidence; as implicit faith; implicit confidence; implicit belief.
scriptures: So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.
John 4:22
Ye worship ye know not what: we know what we worship: for salvation is of the Jews.
For as I passed by, and beheld your devotions, I found an altar with this inscription, TO THE UNKNOWN GOD. Whom therefore ye ignorantly worship, him declare I unto you.
Hos 4:6

My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge: because thou hast rejected knowledge, I will also reject thee, that thou shalt be no priest to me: seeing thou hast forgotten the law of thy God, I will also forget thy children.
But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts: and be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear:
corruption_summary: Faith is made a submission to an institution rather than a trust in a known Christ, and Protestants do it too.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformed objection is not to trusting teachers — God gave pastors and teachers, and no one verifies everything for himself. It is to a faith whose content is whatever they hold, with the believer never required to know what that is. Such a faith cannot be examined, cannot be corrected, and cannot comfort, because comfort comes from what is believed rather than from the act of believing. Romans 10:17 makes the connection unbreakable: faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God, so a faith that has heard nothing in particular has nothing in particular to rest on.

John 4:22 is uncomfortable because the Lord says it to a woman in the middle of a warm conversation, and He does not soften it: ye worship ye know not what. Sincerity is not the issue; the Samaritans were sincere. Content is. He goes on immediately to say that the Father seeketh true worshippers who worship in spirit and in truth, and joins the two so they cannot be separated into a party of warmth and a party of accuracy.

The Protestant form of implicit faith is common and rarely named. A congregation that could not state why it believes what it believes, that holds its doctrine because a trusted man teaches it and would hold the opposite from the same man, has fides implicita with a different institution attached. First Peter 3:15 is addressed to ordinary scattered believers under pressure and assumes they can give a reason — not a seminary lecture, but an account of the hope that is in them. A church that has never equipped its people to do that has left them with a folded-up faith.
roots_summary: Greek pistis (G4102), faith; akoe (G189), hearing, report; gnosis / epignosis (G1108, G1922), knowledge; apologia (G627), a reasoned defence.
roots_lines: Greek pistis ex akoes (G4102, G189) — faith by hearing; Romans 10:14–17.
Greek apologia (G627) — answer, defence; 1 Peter 3:15, Philippians 1:7, 2 Timothy 4:16.
Hebrew da'ath (H1847) — knowledge; Hosea 4:1, 4:6, 6:6, Proverbs 2:5.
usage: “Faith cometh by hearing” — so it always has content.
“Ye worship ye know not what” — said kindly, and not softened.
“A reason of the hope that is in you” — expected of scattered laymen.

pos: adj. (admitting of no excuse or justification; without defence)
etymology: Latin inexcusabilis, from ex-, out, and causa, a cause or plea — to excuse is to plead a man out of his charge. The AV uses the word once, at Romans 2:1.
biblical_def: The word appears once: “Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things” (Rom 2:1). Its companion closes the case against the pagan: God's eternal power and Godhead are seen in the things He made, “so that they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20). The Lord says the same of those who heard Him: “If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin” (John 15:22). The purpose of the whole indictment is stated: “that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God” (Rom 3:19). And knowledge raises the account (Luk 12:47).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inexcusable as not to be excused or justified; as an inexcusable fault, an inexcusable neglect of duty.
webster_full: INEXCUSABLE, a. Not to be excused or justified; as inexcusable folly.
INEXCUSABLENESS, n. The quality of not admitting of excuse or justification.
EXCUSE, v.t. To pardon; to free from the imputation of fault or blame; to acquit of guilt.
scriptures: Rom 2:1
Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things.
Rom 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
John 15:22
If I had not come and spoken unto them, they had not had sin: but now they have no cloke for their sin.
Rom 3:19
Now we know that what things soever the law saith, it saith to them who are under the law: that every mouth may be stopped, and all the world may become guilty before God.
And that servant, which knew his lord's will, and prepared not himself, neither did according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes.
corruption_summary: Romans 2:1 is read as a ban on all moral judgment, and it is an indictment of the man whose judgment is accurate.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular use of this verse gets its logic backwards. Paul does not say the moralist's verdict on the pagan was wrong; he grants it and turns it. Wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things. The problem is not that the standard was misapplied but that it was applied in one direction only, and the man who can see the fault clearly enough to name it has demonstrated that he knows the law he is breaking. Being right about someone else's sin is precisely what leaves him without a defence.

Romans 1:20 and 3:19 together explain why the doctrine matters. The whole first section of Romans is a legal argument working toward a verdict — every mouth stopped, all the world guilty before God — and it must reach that point before 3:21 can say But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested. Grace is unintelligible to a man who still has a plea. This is why preaching that never establishes guilt produces converts who are grateful for improvement rather than for rescue.

Luke 12:47 keeps the doctrine from flattening into a single verdict. The servant who knew his lord's will and did it not shall be beaten with many stripes; he that knew not, with few. Guilt is universal and it is not uniform, and the ones with most to answer for are those who sat under the clearest light. John 15:22 says the same of the men who heard Christ Himself speak: now they have no cloke for their sin. A church member of thirty years hearing sound preaching should find that sobering rather than reassuring.
roots_summary: Greek anapologetos (G379), without excuse, inexcusable; prophasis (G4392), a pretext, cloke; hupodikos (G5267), under judgment, guilty; phrasso (G5420), to stop the mouth.
roots_lines: Greek anapologetos (G379) — without excuse; Romans 1:20, 2:1 — both occurrences.
Greek prophasis (G4392) — pretext, cloke; John 15:22, Matthew 23:14, 1 Thessalonians 2:5.
Greek hupodikos (G5267) — guilty, answerable; Romans 3:19 only.
usage: “Wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself” — the verdict was right.
“That every mouth may be stopped” — and only then, But now.
“They have no cloke for their sin” — of men who had heard Him.

pos: adj. and v. (inserted into another stock so as to live by its root; the AV spells it engrafted and graffed)
etymology: From graft, Old French grafe, a stylus — from the shape of the cut scion. James 1:21 has “the engrafted word”; Romans 11 has graffed five times.
biblical_def: To be ingrafted is to be cut from one stock and set into another, so as to live by a root not one's own. Paul's olive tree is the great figure: the wild branch “wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree” (Rom 11:17), which is contrary to nature (Rom 11:24), and the warning follows at once: “Be not highminded, but fear” (Rom 11:20). The union is the same one Christ names: “I am the vine, ye are the branches: he that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5). James applies the figure to the word itself, “receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls” (Jas 1:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ingraft as to insert a cion of one tree or plant into another for propagation; and figuratively, to set or fix deep and firm.
webster_full: INGRAFT, v.t. To insert a cion of one tree or plant into another for propagation; as, to ingraft a peach on a plum.
2. To plant or introduce something foreign into that which is already established.
3. To set or fix deep and firm; as principles ingrafted in the mind.
scriptures: And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;
Well; because of unbelief they were broken off, and thou standest by faith. Be not highminded, but fear:

For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural branches, be graffed into their own olive tree?
John 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
Jas 1:21
Wherefore lay apart all filthiness and superfluity of naughtiness, and receive with meekness the engrafted word, which is able to save your souls.
corruption_summary: The figure is read as a promotion when Paul wrote it as a warning, and the branch that was graffed in can be cut out.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 11 is addressed to Gentile believers tempted to look down on unbelieving Israel, and every feature of the horticulture is chosen to prevent that. The graffed branch contributes nothing: it does not support the root, the root supports it. Its inclusion is contrary to nature, which is to say abnormal, unearned and surprising. And it happened by faith while others were broken off by unbelief — a mechanism that says nothing whatever about the superiority of the branch. Boast not against the branches: if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee.

Verse 20 puts the doctrine's edge where sentiment would rather not have it: Be not highminded, but fear. Paul argues that if God spared not the natural branches, neither will He spare a presumptuous graft, and the argument is a solemn one addressed to professing Christians rather than a threat to the elect's security. The Reformed have read it as the Bible's ordinary way of speaking to a mixed body — the warning is real, it is one of the means by which the elect persevere, and a man who hears it and shrugs is exactly the one it was written for.

James adds the personal side of the figure. The engrafted word is one that has been set into a man so that it lives there, not one he has heard and admired; and he says receive it with meekness, because a graft requires a wound in the stock and the stock does not choose the shape of the cut. That is why the next verses are about being doers and not hearers only, and about the man who beholds his natural face in a glass and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was.
roots_summary: Greek egkentrizo (G1461), to graft in; emphutos (G1721), implanted, engrafted; ekklao (G1575), to break off; meno (G3306), to abide.
roots_lines: Greek egkentrizo (G1461) — to graft in; Romans 11:17, 11:19, 11:23–24 — all six occurrences are in this chapter.
Greek emphutos (G1721) — implanted, engrafted; James 1:21 only.
Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, remain; John 15:4–7, 1 John 2:6, 2:28.
usage: “Thou bearest not the root, but the root thee” — the whole argument in a clause.
“Be not highminded, but fear” — written to Christians.
“Receive with meekness the engrafted word” — a graft needs a wound.

pos: adj. (descending by inheritance; passed from parent to child — in Calvin, of the corruption every man receives from Adam)
etymology: Latin hereditarius, from heres, an heir. Calvin's phrase is hereditary corruption: what we inherit from our first father is not merely his example but his nature.
biblical_def: Sin is hereditary in that it is received by descent, not acquired by imitation. David traces it behind his own memory: “Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me” (Psa 51:5). Job states the impossibility: “Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one” (Job 14:4). Paul gives the channel: “by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned” (Rom 5:12). The result is a standing condition, not a record of acts: we “were by nature the children of wrath, even as others” (Eph 2:3). And Genesis marks the transmission in the genealogy itself: Adam “begat a son in his own likeness, after his image” (Gen 5:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hereditary as descending by inheritance; that may descend from an ancestor to an heir; and, of qualities or diseases, transmitted from a parent to a child.
webster_full: HEREDITARY, a. That has descended from an ancestor to an heir; that descends by inheritance, or comes by right of inheritance; as an hereditary estate; an hereditary crown.
2. That is or may be transmitted from a parent to a child; as hereditary pride, hereditary bravery, hereditary disease.
scriptures: Psa 51:5
Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.
Job 14:4
Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? not one.
Rom 5:12
Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned:
Eph 2:3
Among whom also we all had our conversation in times past in the lusts of our flesh, fulfilling the desires of the flesh and of the mind; and were by nature the children of wrath, even as others.
Gen 5:3
And Adam lived an hundred and thirty years, and begat a son in his own likeness, after his image; and called his name Seth:
corruption_summary: Original sin is reduced to a bad example we copy, and Scripture makes it a nature we receive.
corruption_paragraphs: Pelagius taught that Adam harmed his posterity by setting a precedent, so that sin spreads by imitation and a man could in principle live without it. The reply is Genesis 5:3, which says of Adam what Genesis 1 had said of God: Adam begat a son in his own likeness, after his image. The image-language moves down the genealogy, and what is transmitted is a nature, not a habit. Psalm 51:5 makes the same point from the inside: David, confessing a specific adult sin, reaches behind every act he can remember to the condition he was conceived in. He is not excusing the act; he is explaining that the act came from somewhere.

The doctrine offends because it appears to convict a man of something he did not do, and the offence should not be smoothed over. The Reformed answer is federal: Adam acted as the head of the race under a covenant, as Christ acted as the head of a new one, and Romans 5 sets the two in parallel precisely so that the second may be understood by the first. Anyone who dismantles the imputation of Adam's sin has, by the same argument, dismantled the imputation of Christ's righteousness — they stand or fall together, and Paul's whole point is that the ruin and the rescue work the same way.

Pastorally the doctrine explains what parents already know. No child requires instruction in selfishness, deceit or resentment; the labour of raising them runs entirely in the other direction. Ephesians 2:3 says by nature the children of wrath, and adds even as others, which removes the last refuge, since the well-behaved are in the same clause as the scandalous. That is why the same chapter can say, two verses later, But God, who is rich in mercy — a sentence that means nothing until the first three verses are believed.
roots_summary: Hebrew chul (H2342), to be brought forth; yacham (H3179), to conceive; Greek phusis (G5449), nature; eiserchomai (G1525), to enter in.
roots_lines: Hebrew demuth / tselem (H1823, H6754) — likeness, image; Genesis 1:26–27, 5:1–3.
Greek phusis (G5449) — nature; Ephesians 2:3, Romans 2:14, 11:24, Galatians 2:15.
Greek dierchomai eis pantas (G1330) — passed upon all; Romans 5:12.
usage: “In sin did my mother conceive me” — behind every act he could remember.
“Begat a son in his own likeness” — the image-language moves down the line.
“By nature the children of wrath, even as others” — the last refuge removed.

pos: adj. (that cannot be overcome; unconquerable — in controversy, of an ignorance held to excuse the ignorant)
etymology: Latin invincibilis, from vincere, to conquer. Rome's invincible ignorance is an ignorance a man could not have removed, and is held to excuse him; the Reformed reply is that Scripture excuses no one on that ground.
biblical_def: Invincible means unconquerable. In the doctrinal dispute the question is whether ignorance excuses, and Scripture's answer is layered. It reduces guilt: “he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes” (Luk 12:48); Paul “obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief” (1Ti 1:13); Peter grants that “through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers” (Act 3:17). It does not acquit: the same Peter goes on to say “Repent ye therefore”, and God “now commandeth all men every where to repent” (Act 17:30). And the general revelation leaves men “without excuse” (Rom 1:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines invincible as not to be conquered or subdued; unconquerable; insuperable; as an invincible army, or an invincible obstacle.
webster_full: INVINCIBLE, a. Not to be conquered or subdued; unconquerable; insuperable; as an invincible army; invincible love or hatred; invincible difficulty.
INVINCIBLENESS, n. The quality of being invincible; unconquerableness.
scriptures: But he that knew not, and did commit things worthy of stripes, shall be beaten with few stripes. For unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required: and to whom men have committed much, of him they will ask the more.
Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
Act 3:17
And now, brethren, I wot that through ignorance ye did it, as did also your rulers.
And the times of this ignorance God winked at; but now commandeth all men every where to repent:
Rom 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
corruption_summary: Ignorance is made an acquittal or made no defence at all, and Scripture treats it as neither.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors face each other here. The first turns ignorance into a verdict of not guilty, so that the unevangelised are safe and evangelism becomes a risk rather than a rescue — a position Romans 1 forecloses, since men are said to be without excuse on the strength of creation alone, and Romans 10 asks how they shall believe in Him of whom they have not heard. The second denies any distinction at all, flattening Luke 12:47–48 where the Lord Himself distinguishes many stripes from few. Both errors reach a tidy result by ignoring half the evidence.

The Reformed position holds the tension the text holds. Guilt is universal and degrees of guilt are real. Paul, who calls himself the chief of sinners for persecuting the church, says he obtained mercy because I did it ignorantly in unbelief — and note what the ignorance secures: not innocence but mercy, and mercy is only ever given to the guilty. Peter tells the crowd that they killed the Prince of life through ignorance, and the sentence that follows is not therefore you are excused but repent ye therefore, and be converted.

Acts 17:30 is the hinge verse and it has been misread in both directions. The times of this ignorance God winked at — overlooked, forbore — but now commandeth all men every where to repent. There is a real divine forbearance toward what men did not know, and it is past tense; the command that replaces it is present, universal and addressed to everyone the message reaches. Which is precisely why the message must be carried.
roots_summary: Greek agnoia (G52), ignorance; agnoeo (G50), to be ignorant; hupereidon (G5237), to overlook, wink at; anapologetos (G379), without excuse.
roots_lines: Greek agnoia (G52) — ignorance; Acts 3:17, 17:30, Ephesians 4:18, 1 Peter 1:14.
Greek hupereidon (G5237) — overlooked, winked at; Acts 17:30 only.
Greek anapologetos (G379) — without excuse; Romans 1:20, 2:1.
usage: “Shall be beaten with few stripes” — few, and still beaten.
“I did it ignorantly” — and what it secured was mercy, not innocence.
“God… now commandeth all men every where to repent” — the forbearance is past tense.
